entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Dōkyō (700 CE – May 17, 772 CE) was a powerful Japanese Buddhist monk who exerted immense political influence during the Nara period, particularly through his intimate relationship with Empress Kōken, who reigned twice as Empress Kōken (749–758) and Empress Shōtoku (764–770). Rising from a modest background in the Wakae district, Dōkyō became a central figure in court politics, ultimately holding unprecedented titles such as Daijō-daijin Zenji (Grand Minister of State and Zen Master) and Hōō (Dharma King), positioning himself at the very pinnacle of both the religious and secular worlds of 8th-century Japan. His ambition to ascend to the imperial throne itself, a move that fundamentally challenged the established imperial succession, makes him a pivotal, albeit controversial, figure in early Japanese history.

Dōkyō's rise began in the mid-760s when Empress Kōken, after abdicating and then resuming the throne as Empress Shōtoku, became increasingly devoted to Buddhism and relied heavily on his spiritual counsel. He quickly consolidated power, overseeing significant state affairs and even attempting to relocate the capital from Nara to Yuge, near his home province, in 769 CE. His most audacious move was his bid for the imperial throne, which he attempted to legitimize through a fabricated oracle from the Usa Hachiman Shrine in Kyushu. This was famously thwarted by Wake no Kiyomaro, who, after consulting the shrine directly, returned with a message declaring that only a person of imperial lineage could rule Japan, leading to Dōkyō's rapid political decline.
